_about: The AES walk's words (docs/walkthrough-design.md sections 2.2, 2.2c, 2.6). acceptance/checks/docs_checks.py scans this file for the phrases of section 2.6 and for the field definition lines.
fill: This is the block: 16 bytes of the text. They go down the columns, 4 bytes to a column. Next adds one byte.
decryptStart: Encrypt is done, and this is the locked block. Decrypt now runs the inverse steps, in reverse order, to get the text back.

steps.AddRoundKey: Each byte is XORed with the byte in the same place of round key {round}.
steps.SubBytes: Each byte is looked up in the S-box table, and the value there takes its place.
steps.ShiftRows: Row 0 stays. Rows 1, 2 and 3 rotate left by 1, 2 and 3 bytes. The name says shift, but no byte is lost: FIPS 197 calls it a cyclic shift, the same idea as a rotate left (ROL).
steps.MixColumns: Each column is multiplied by a fixed matrix in the AES field, so every byte of a column now depends on all 4 bytes of that column.
steps.InvShiftRows: Each row moves back to the right by the places ShiftRows moved it to the left.
steps.InvSubBytes: Each byte is looked up in the inverse S-box table, which undoes the S-box.
steps.InvMixColumns: Each column is multiplied by the inverse matrix, which undoes MixColumns.

wire.notSent: A teaching example. AES runs on this text block alone, the way ECB uses it. This run did not send this block in ECB.
wire.match: This run sent this block in ECB. The locked block on the wire equals the walk's output.
wire.differs: This run sent this block in ECB, and a tamper plan changed it on the wire. The walk shows the block the sender locked.

keys.title: Key schedule
keys.start: The key makes one round key for each AddRoundKey. The first words are the key itself. Next builds each later word from two earlier words.
keys.eachRound: Each round gets its own key.
keys.only128: Round keys are key material. Anyone who learns one round key can run this table backward and get the key.
keys.decrypt: Decryption uses the same round keys, from last to first.
keys.band192: The first 6 words are the key, so round key 1 starts with key bytes.
keys.band256: The first 8 words are the key, so round key 1 is all key bytes.
keys.keyNote: This word is part of the key, so nothing is calculated.
keys.rcon: Round constants. Each value is the one before it, doubled in the field. The list starts at 01. No key goes in, so every AES key uses this same list.
keys.tapHint: Each column is one word. Tap a built word to see how it was made.
keys.rotCopy: RotWord works on a copy of w{prev}, so w{prev} itself does not change. The copy moves up one byte, and the top byte wraps to the bottom. All 4 bytes of w{i} then use this one finished copy.
keys.subCopy: AES-256 only: a copy of w{prev} goes through the S-box, with no rotation. w{prev} itself does not change.
keys.fillsKey: The key fills w0 to w{last}

sbox.pick: Click a byte in the grid. Its first digit picks the row and its second digit picks the column.
sbox.facts: 8 bits in, 8 bits out, 256 entries. One table for every byte, round, and key. It is public and holds no secret: the key enters only through AddRoundKey.
sbox.inverse: The inverse table undoes the swap. The S-box is not its own inverse, so decryption needs this second table.

field.pick: Click a byte in the grid to see the 4 products that made it.
field.reduced: too big for a byte, so it is reduced by 11b

closed: Show keys is off. These steps show the key and the round keys, so they stay closed. Turn Show keys on to walk them. The S-box table below and the modes walk stay open.
definition: A field is a set of values with add, subtract, multiply and divide, where every answer stays in the set. Only divide by zero is not allowed. They follow the usual rules of arithmetic.
A finite field has a fixed number of values. Another name for it is a Galois field. The field that AES uses has 256 values, one for each byte. Its name is GF(2^8).
Multiply treats each byte as a polynomial, multiplies without carries, and reduces the result by x^8 + x^4 + x^3 + x + 1 (11b in hex). So the answer always fits in a byte.
Every value except zero has an inverse. So multiplying by any nonzero value can be undone.
